content.text: RH134: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 System Administration II
This chapter teaches you two important things:
Firewall: Control which network connections can reach your Linux server.
SELinux port labeling: Control which network ports a service is allowed to use.

We will follow your tutor format: small concepts, simple explanations, real commands, explanations of each command part, and practical labs. The book uses RHEL 8, so I will point out where your RHEL 10 lab may differ.
Part 2: Guided Exercise — Managing Server Firewalls
Part 4: Guided Exercise — Controlling SELinux Port Labeling
Part 5: Final Performance Lab — Managing Network Security
Main idea: A firewall controls which network traffic is allowed to enter or pass through a computer.
Imagine your Linux server is a building. The firewall is the security guard at the entrance. The guard checks incoming connections and allows only traffic permitted by the rules.
For example, a web server usually needs to accept connections on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. If those ports are blocked, people might not be able to open your website.
sudo — run the command with administrator privileges.
firewall-cmd — the command-line tool for managing firewalld.
--list-all — display the firewall settings for a zone, including allowed services and ports.
What happens: You see the active zone's settings, including which services and ports are allowed.
Remember: A service can be running correctly but remain unreachable because the firewall blocks its connections.
Main idea: Linux checks network packets using its kernel networking framework before the packets reach their destination.
A packet is a small unit of data sent over a network. Imagine each packet as a delivery package.
Linux uses Netfilter, a framework inside the Linux kernel, to inspect and handle packets. It can allow, reject, drop, or modify traffic, depending on the rules.

RHEL 8 uses nftables as its modern packet-filtering system. The nft command manages its rules. firewalld provides a simpler way to manage firewall rules without requiring you to write low-level rules yourself.
Think of the relationship this way:
firewalld: The manager that helps you configure those rules.
systemctl — manages and checks system services.
What happens: You can see whether the firewall service is running.
Remember: Netfilter handles packets, nftables supplies rules, and firewalld helps you manage them.

sections.title: 3. Why use firewalld instead of older tools?

content.text: Main idea: firewalld makes firewall management easier by using zones and predefined services.
Older tools such as iptables and ip6tables were commonly used to configure Linux firewalls. RHEL 8 uses nftables as the modern replacement, and firewalld is the recommended management tool.
Imagine managing building security. Instead of writing separate instructions for every door, you create security areas with predefined rules.
That is the idea behind firewalld zones. You can assign a network connection to a zone and control the traffic allowed through that zone.
What happens: You see zone names such as public, home, work, trusted, and others.
The exact available zones can depend on the installed configuration.
Remember: Zones let you manage groups of firewall rules instead of creating every rule separately.
Main idea: A zone is a group of firewall rules that defines which incoming connections are allowed.
Imagine your server has different security settings for your home network, office network, and an untrusted public network. A zone lets you apply different rules to each situation.
For example, you might allow more services on a trusted home network but only SSH on a public network.
Here are the predefined zones described in the RHEL 8 book:
Allows selected services, including SSH, mDNS, printing, Samba client, and DHCPv6 client.
Allows selected services, including SSH, printing, and DHCPv6 client.
Intended for untrusted public networks; SSH and DHCPv6 client are initially allowed.
For networks where outgoing IPv4 traffic may need masquerading.
For servers that need limited incoming access from external networks.
Rejects incoming traffic that is not related to outgoing connections.
Silently discards incoming traffic that is not related to outgoing connections.
These are initial defaults; administrators can change the rules.
This displays the default zone, often public on a standard setup.
Remember: Choose a zone based on how much trust you place in the network.
Main idea: The default zone is the zone firewalld uses when traffic has not been assigned to another zone.
Think of a default zone as the default security policy for a visitor when no special rule identifies them.
Firewalld determines which zone applies using rules such as these:
If a source IP address has been assigned to a zone, that zone applies.
Otherwise, the zone assigned to the incoming network interface applies.
If neither assignment applies, firewalld uses the default zone.
An interface is a network connection, such as ens160. A source IP identifies the machine or network sending traffic.
This command changes the runtime and permanent default zone.
Remember: The default zone is a designation; it is not a separate firewall zone of its own.
Main idea: A firewalld service is a named set of network ports and protocols needed by an application.
Imagine a service name as a shortcut. Instead of remembering every port used by an application, you can allow the named service.
For example, the ssh service allows the standard SSH connection on TCP port 22.
A protocol is the agreed method used for communication. TCP and UDP are two common transport protocols.
What happens: Firewalld lists the predefined service names available on your system.
Their service definitions are normally stored in:
Remember: A service name saves you from manually specifying its port and protocol.

sections.title: 7. Allow a service through the firewall

content.text: Main idea: Adding a service to a zone allows the network traffic defined by that service.
Suppose SSH is not allowed by the rules of your chosen zone. Adding the ssh service allows the connection covered by that service definition.
--add-service=http — allow the predefined HTTP service in the default zone.
This command changes the runtime configuration. That means the rule is applied now but is not automatically saved for future restarts.
To apply permanent changes to the running firewall:
Remember: Runtime changes apply now; permanent changes are saved and can be loaded into the running firewall.
Main idea: You can allow a specific port and protocol without using a predefined service name.
Suppose an application listens on TCP port 1001, but there is no convenient predefined service for it. You can open that port directly.
--permanent — save the rule in permanent configuration.
/tcp — the protocol used by the port.
The port must also be used by a running application, and SELinux must permit the application to use it.
Remember: Opening a firewall port does not start an application or override SELinux restrictions.
Main idea: You can remove firewall permissions that are no longer required.
If your server no longer provides a website, you might remove its HTTP permission. Think of this as removing a key from the security guard's approved list.
Example — remove HTTP from the runtime configuration:
--remove-service=http — removes permission for the HTTP service.
--remove-port=1001/tcp — removes the specified TCP port rule.
--reload — loads the saved configuration into the running firewall.
If you remove a rule only from runtime, a previously saved permanent rule may reappear after reloading.
Remember: Remove unnecessary permissions, but do not accidentally block SSH or another connection you need to administer the server.
Main idea: Firewalld keeps active rules and saved rules, and they are not always identical.
Think of runtime configuration as the instructions currently being used by the security guard. Permanent configuration is the saved instruction sheet.
If you add a runtime rule, it takes effect immediately but may disappear after a reload or restart. If you add a permanent rule, it is saved but normally needs a reload before it affects runtime.
--reload — applies the saved configuration to runtime.
--list-services — displays services allowed in the runtime zone.
Important: The --set-default-zone command is an exception to the usual pattern: it changes both runtime and permanent configuration.
Remember: For a lasting firewall change, save it permanently and then reload when required.

sections.title: 11. List zones and inspect their rules

content.text: Main idea: Inspecting firewall configuration helps you understand where traffic is allowed.
Before changing security rules, check the current configuration. Otherwise, you might remove an important permission or open the wrong zone.
--get-active-zones — shows zones currently in use and their associated interfaces or sources.
--list-all — shows the rules for the default zone.
--list-all-zones — shows the rules for all zones.
Here, --zone=public selects the public zone rather than the default zone.
Remember: Inspect the correct zone before changing it.

sections.title: 12. Assign a network interface to a zone

content.text: Main idea: An interface can be associated with a zone to apply that zone's rules to incoming traffic on the interface.
Imagine a building with separate entrances. Each entrance can have its own security policy. A network interface is like an entrance through which packets arrive.

To make an interface assignment permanent, use the permanent option and follow the NetworkManager/firewalld configuration method appropriate for your system. Interface assignments may be managed through NetworkManager, so verify the result rather than assuming the runtime command persists.
Remember: Assign interfaces carefully: the wrong zone can expose services or block required connections.

sections.title: 13. Assign a source network to a zone

content.text: Main idea: You can apply firewall rules to traffic coming from a particular source IP address or network.
Instead of assigning rules to a physical entrance, you can identify visitors by their originating network.
For example, you might place traffic from 192.168.1.0/24 in the internal zone. The /24 is CIDR notation: it describes a network containing addresses in that subnet.
--add-source=192.168.1.0/24 — associate that source network with the zone.
To remove the source assignment, use --remove-source with the same network and zone.
Remember: Source-based zone assignment identifies traffic by where it comes from, not by which interface it uses.

sections.title: 14. Set the default zone and reload the firewall

content.text: Main idea: You can change the default zone and reload firewall rules when needed.
This makes dmz the default zone. Use it only if that matches your intended security design.
Why this matters: A reload is often necessary after adding or removing permanent services, ports, or source assignments. It applies the saved configuration without requiring a full system reboot.

The book also describes configuring firewall services through the Web Console. You can open the server's Cockpit interface, go to Networking → Firewall, choose the relevant zone, and add the service you need. The exact screen can vary with the installed Cockpit version.
Remember: Check the zone and existing rules before making a change, and verify the result afterward.

sections.title: 15. Understand the purpose of the exercise

content.text: Main idea: You will configure a web server so HTTPS works while HTTP remains blocked by the firewall.
The exercise uses servera as a web server. You install the web service, create a test page, and check whether the page is reachable over HTTP and HTTPS.
HTTP uses TCP port 80. HTTPS uses TCP port 443 and encrypts the web connection.
The exercise demonstrates an important difference: installing and starting a service does not automatically mean the firewall permits access to it.

Main idea: SELinux adds security checks that can prevent a service from doing something even when normal Linux permissions allow it.

Imagine the firewall as the security guard at the building entrance. SELinux is the permission system inside the building. Even if a visitor gets through the entrance, the permission system can still stop them from entering a restricted room.
SELinux can restrict which ports a service is allowed to use. This helps prevent an unexpected or misconfigured application from taking over a network port.
For example, Apache normally serves HTTP on TCP port 80 and HTTPS on TCP port 443. If you configure Apache to listen on another port, SELinux may need an appropriate port label.
getenforce — displays the current SELinux mode.
Enforcing — SELinux actively enforces its rules.
Remember: The firewall controls network access, while SELinux controls what a service is permitted to do.

sections.title: 21. What is an SELinux port label?

content.text: Main idea: A port label identifies the security type assigned to a network port.
SELinux labels help the operating system decide which services can use particular resources. A port label is like a sign on a door that identifies what kind of access is appropriate.
The suffix _t indicates an SELinux type. The type is part of SELinux's security labeling system.
If Apache tries to listen on a port that is not labeled appropriately, SELinux can deny the action—even when the firewall permits the port.
semanage port -l — lists SELinux port assignments.
| — sends the first command's output to the next command.
grep http — displays lines containing http.
Remember: Before changing SELinux port rules, check the existing label.
Main idea: semanage manages parts of SELinux policy, including port labels.
A policy is a set of security rules. semanage lets an administrator make supported changes to those rules without manually rewriting the entire SELinux policy.
The output identifies the SELinux type, protocol, and port numbers assigned to it.
The -C option shows local customizations rather than simply listing the full policy.
If the command is missing, the required administration tools may not be installed. On RHEL systems, the package is commonly policycoreutils-python-utils.
Remember: Use semanage port -l to inspect port labels before making changes.
Main idea: You can assign an appropriate SELinux type to a port that a service needs to use.
-t http_port_t — choose the HTTP port type.
This allows port 82 to use the http_port_t label, which is suitable for web-server ports.
Important: This command may fail if the port already has an assignment that conflicts with the requested change. Inspect the current rules before changing anything.
Remember: The label must be suitable for the service; do not label a port merely to silence an error.

sections.title: 24. Modify or remove a port label

content.text: Main idea: Use the appropriate semanage option to add, change, or remove a local port assignment.

sections.title: 35. What if the website still does not work?

content.text: Main idea: Check each layer separately instead of changing random settings.
Is Apache listening on a port?
Think of a website connection as a journey through several checkpoints:
Apache must listen on the correct port.
SELinux must permit Apache to use that port.
The firewall must allow incoming traffic.
The client must connect to the correct address and port.
A failure at any checkpoint can prevent access.
If this fails, inspect the service, port, SELinux, and firewall settings. Do not immediately disable security features.
Remember: Diagnose the failing layer and fix that layer only.
Main idea: The book teaches RHEL 8, so verify commands and package availability on your RHEL 10 system.

The fundamental ideas in this chapter—firewall zones, ports, SELinux labels, and service troubleshooting—remain useful. However, versions can differ in installed packages, defaults, and available tools.
This checks whether firewalld is running.
If semanage is unavailable, check whether its supporting package is installed before continuing.
RHEL 8 uses nftables through firewalld by default.
Your RHEL 10 installation may have different default firewall rules or zone assignments.
The training commands lab ... start, grade, and finish require the course lab environment; they are not general-purpose RHEL commands.
Do not copy the lab's security changes to your everyday machine without understanding their effects.
Remember: Learn the book's expected behavior, then verify your own system before applying changes.

Firewall: Controls which network connections are allowed.
Netfilter: Linux kernel framework that handles network packets.
firewalld: Manages firewall rules using zones and services.
Zone: A group of firewall rules for a type of network connection.
Service: A predefined set of ports and protocols.
Permanent: Rules saved for future use.
SELinux: Adds security restrictions on what services can do.
SELinux port label: Identifies the security type assigned to a network port.
semanage port: Lists and changes SELinux port assignments.
The most important lesson is that a network service needs to be running, permitted by SELinux, and reachable through the firewall. When troubleshooting, check each of those conditions separately.
